title: Graceful GPU Preemption and Prewarming Guidelines
author: Priya Shah
body:
Overview:

This document defines the recommended runtime and infrastructure standards for handling GPU preemption (spot/interruptible instances, cloud maintenance) and for prewarming execution slots in Redwood inference pools. Goal: minimize user-visible errors and latency regressions while preserving cost efficiency. Applies to: hosted and dedicated GPU pools, Dedicated autoscalers, and Private deployment automation where interruptible GPUs may be used.

Why this matters:
- GPU preemption is a common cost optimization (spot/interruptible). If handled poorly, preemption causes request errors, cold-start latency, and state loss (KV cache, model warmup).
- Prewarming warm pools reduces cold-start amplification on traffic spikes and supports SLO stability.

Principles:
1) Fast, observable handoff: preemption should trigger deterministic graceful-shutdown windows and observable signals.
2) Preserve model working set: persist or checkpoint KV cache and other ephemeral state as required by model SLAs.
3) Asymmetric cost model: prioritize critical low-latency routes for reserved (non-interruptible) capacity and permit batch/elastic workloads to use interruptible nodes.
4) Automated recovery and admission control: autoscaler and scheduler must consider warm pool size, in-flight request draining, and admission thresholds.

SLO and thresholds (example targets - tune per-customer):
- Target availability for production routes: 99.95% monthly (exclude scheduled maintenance).
- Latency SLO for interactive routes: p50 < 30ms, p95 < 250ms; cold-start allowance: additional 1500ms for <1% of tokens.
- Preemption drain window requirement: min 45s SIGTERM window (60s recommended) before instance termination.
- Warm pool min sizing heuristic: max(2, floor(0.05 * replica_count)) with a floor of 2 GPUs per pool.

Signals and integration points:
- Cloud provider signals: GCP Preemptible 'TERMINATE' notice, AWS Spot interruption notice (two-minute warning), Azure Spot/maintenance notifications. Map each cloud signal to the same local lifecycle path.
- Cluster orchestrator: for k8s-based Dedicated/Private clusters, rely on preStop hooks and Pod lifecycle events to drain. For non-k8s orchestration, ensure a comparable lifecycle API exists.
- Redwood control plane: control-plane should expose a preemption event webhook that downstream components (autoscaler, router, cache manager) subscribe to.

Graceful shutdown sequence (ordered):
1) Receive preemption signal.
2) Mark node "draining" in scheduler and remove from routing pools for new requests.
3) Immediately capture KV cache snapshot to durable store if model state lifetime > 30s. Use asynchronous flush with confirmation (see persistence policy).
4) Finish in-flight requests within a hard deadline (default 45s). Long-running requests beyond deadline should be cut over to fallback routing: retry to compatible variant (smaller/quantized model) or queue for retry.
5) Evict ephemeral processes and run final health/metrics flush.
6) Release node.

KV cache and working set persistence:
- Persist only when necessary: large context models (context > 8k tokens) and long-running chat sessions require KV checkpointing.
- Snapshot policy: incremental append to object store (S3/GCS) using per-shard checkpointing. Each snapshot must complete within 20s to be effective for preemption windows. If snapshot cannot be completed, fallback to non-persistent strategy and mark traced requests as potentially "cold" in analytics.
- Retention and hygiene: keep last 3 snapshots per model-shard, TTL 1 hour by default.

Prewarming strategies:
A) Warm pool (preferred for low-latency routes): maintain a small number of pre-initialized VM/GPU instances with model artifacts loaded and an empty KV cache. Warm pool sizing: see heuristic above. Warm pools are paid capacity and should be reserved only for routes with strict latency SLOs.
B) Lazy-warm with fast-preload: maintain pre-pulled model artifacts and quantized weights on local disk cache. Boot workflow: launch container -> mount artifact -> start runtime -> accept traffic. Target bootstrap time: < 20s for 7B-class models on NVidia H100-like hardware.
C) Shared warm containers: run multiple lightweight worker processes per GPU to amortize warmup cost for small models.

Admission control and routing policies:
- Tag routes by latency-critical vs elastic. Latency-critical routes must be routed to reserved or warm nodes only. Elastic routes may be routed to interruptible instances with best-effort latency.
- Router should implement immediate fallback: if selected node is draining or preempted, route to next compatible node and, if not available, fallback to smaller model variant or enqueue request with a bounded retry.
- Throttling thresholds: if warm pool saturation > 85% and queue > 100 requests, trigger auto-increment policy to create additional warm instances (see autoscaler section).

Autoscaler integration (recommended config fields):
- warmPool.minSize: integer
- warmPool.scaleFactor: float (0.0-1.0, fraction of steady-state replicas to keep warm)
- preemptionDrainWindowSec: integer (default 60)
- snapshot.timeoutSec: integer (default 20)
- fallbackModelOrder: list (ordered model ids to try when primary unavailable)

Example autoscaler YAML (conceptual):

warmPool:
  minSize: 3
  scaleFactor: 0.05
  maxBurst: 10
preemption:
  drainWindowSec: 60
  snapshotTimeoutSec: 20
fallbackModelOrder: ["redwood-small-quant", "redwood-medium-quant", "redwood-legacy-small"]

Commands and operational recipes:
- Force warm pool resize (example CLI):
  rctl warmpool set --pool inference-nyc-a --min 4
- Trigger manual snapshot flush for model shard: 
  rctl model snapshot flush --model-id redwood-34b --shard 2 --timeout 30s
- Observe draining nodes: 
  rctl nodes list --filter state=draining --output table

Testing and validation checklist (pre-merge for changes):
1) Unit tests for lifecycle handlers and snapshot logic.
2) Staging preemption simulation: inject synthetic preemption signals and assert that no more than 0.5% of requests fail for interactive routes and that cold-start percentiles are within tolerance.
3) Load test with warm pool at target sizing: validate p95 latency and error budget.
4) Chaos test: randomly terminate 5% of warm nodes and verify fallback routing and autoscaler ramp.

Rollout plan for changes to these guidelines/software: 
1) Draft changes in feature branch; unit + integration tests passing.
2) Canary deploy to low-traffic region (Region: us-west-2 / pool: canary-warm-1) for 48 hours.
3) Monitor metrics: preemption-induced 5xx rate, cold start percentiles, warm pool utilization.
4) Gradual 20/40/100% rollout to remaining pools with 24-hour observation windows.

Operational runbook (immediate actions on preemption spikes):
1) Check control-plane alerts: preemption events per-minute > X (threshold).
2) If warmPool utilization > 90%: increase warmpool.minSize by +2 and scale up reserved instances.
3) If snapshot timeouts occur: disable persistence for affected model shards and escalate to runtime team.
4) If p95 latency > SLO for > 10 minutes: enable emergency routing to lower-cost quantized model variant and notify product owners.

Ownership and responsibilities:
- Runtime team: implement graceful shutdown hooks, snapshot API, and KV flush logic.
- Infra autoscaler team: expose warmPool config and implement scale policies.
- Router/service-mesh team: implement drain-aware routing and fallback logic.
- Observability team: provide dashboards and alerts (see Observability section).

Observability and alerts (minimum set):
- preemption.events.rate (per-pool) -> alert when > 5/min for 15m
- warmpool.utilization (per-pool) -> warn at > 85% for 10m, critical at > 95%
- snapshot.failure.rate (per-model-shard) -> alert at > 1%
- runtime.shutdown.durations -> SLO: 95% < drainWindowSec

Metrics dashboards (recommended panels):
- Warm pool capacity vs active queries
- Cold-start percentile heatmap by model family and region
- Snapshot latency histogram and failure counts
- Routing fallback counts and fallback model latency

Security and cost notes:
- Warm pools increase baseline cost. Use route tagging and cost allocation to bill back customers.
- Snapshot data must be stored encrypted-at-rest using customer or Redwood-managed KMS depending on privacy/confidentiality.

Appendix A — Example k8s preStop snippet (for k8s-based deployments):

# preStop: give the process time to drain and snapshot
preStop:
  exec:
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "/opt/redwood/bin/drain-and-snapshot --timeout=45"]

Appendix B — Small model boot sequence (timings observed in staging):
- Container start: 1.2s
- Artifact mount and checksum: 1.0s
- Runtime warm init (weights mmap / cuda init): 6.8s
- Accept traffic: ~9.0s total
